name: Queenstown
tagline: Alpine adventure capital on a glacial mountain lake.
bestMonths: Jan, Feb, Mar, Sep, Oct, Nov and Dec
whenBlurb: December to March delivers warm, long-lit days for the lake and hikes; June to August is ski season with the Winter Festival, and April brings Arrowtown's gold - there is no truly bad time.

ourTake.lede: Queenstown is an adrenaline town that quietly does luxury very well, the trick is to balance one big adventure day against slower time on the lake and in the wine country next door. Base in or near the centre for the first night, then consider decamping to the quieter side of the lake. Central Otago's wineries are half the reason to come and most people underrate them; don't.
ourTake.comeIf: You want mountains and lakes with adventure or fine wine at the doorstep.
ourTake.skipIf: You want a short-haul trip; New Zealand is a long way for anything under a week.

guide.lede: Where to stay, what to do, where to eat, and where the night goes, grouped by price, every address earned by a name worth trusting.

items.name: Rosewood Matakauri
credentials: MICHELIN One Key (2025)
Travel + Leisure World's Best Awards 2024, Top 100 Hotels in the World (No. 45)
Condé Nast Traveler Gold List / Readers' Choice
items.description: A tiny Rosewood lodge above Lake Wakatipu, three suites and four villas in the beech forest, service to rival any city house.

items.name: Blanket Bay
credentials: MICHELIN Two Keys (2025)
Relais & Châteaux
Small Luxury Hotels of the World
items.description: A great stone-and-timber lodge on the shore of Lake Wakatipu beneath the Humboldt range, the archetype of the New Zealand high-country lodge.

items.name: The Lindis
credentials: MICHELIN Two Keys (2025)
items.description: An architectural marvel under a slatted timber roof in a remote high-country valley, pods and suites dissolving into the landscape.

items.name: Eichardt's Private Hotel
credentials: MICHELIN One Key (2025)
Small Luxury Hotels of the World
items.description: The best few rooms in town, an 1861 lakefront landmark on Marine Parade, run as an intimate private hotel.

items.name: Gibbston Valley Lodge & Spa
credentials: MICHELIN One Key (2025)
items.description: Standalone villas set among organic Pinot Noir vines, beside the region's original wine cave and its landmark winery.

items.name: Azur Lodge
credentials: MICHELIN One Key (2025)
items.description: Nine private hilltop villas with floor-to-ceiling glass framing Lake Wakatipu and the Remarkables, seclusion two miles from town.

items.name: Whare Kea Lodge & Chalet
credentials: Relais & Châteaux
items.description: A six-room lakeside lodge on the shore of Lake Wanaka, with its own alpine chalet high in the Buchanan range for heli-guests.

items.name: Sofitel Queenstown Hotel & Spa
credentials: MICHELIN Guide, Selected
items.description: French polish in the heart of the village, the most refined full-service city hotel in Queenstown proper.

items.name: Hulbert House
credentials: MICHELIN Guide, Selected
items.description: A restored 1888 Victorian villa turned eight-room boutique hotel, the grand private-residence feel, above the village.

items.name: Stoneridge Estate
credentials: MICHELIN Guide, Selected
items.description: An alpine retreat and vineyard on the shores of Lake Hayes, five-star calm between Queenstown and Arrowtown.

items.name: QT Queenstown
credentials: MICHELIN Guide, Selected
items.description: A design-led, playful house near the lakefront, style and a good bar at a gentler price.

items.name: Skyline Gondola & Bob's Peak
items.description: The steepest cable-car lift in the Southern Hemisphere climbs 480m in about ten minutes to a glass-fronted eyrie over Lake Wakatipu, with The Remarkables and Cecil and Walter Peaks laid out across the water. Ride up for a leisurely buffet at the Stratosfare Restaurant, or simply for the sundowner view, gentle enough for the grandparents, spectacular for everyone.

items.name: The Skyline Luge
items.description: At the top of the gondola, gravity carts wind down banked, tunnelled tracks with 220-degree views of the lake and mountains, the Blue Track a gentle cruise, the Red Track steeper and faster. It is the rare thrill that a nine-year-old and a grandfather can both take on, at their own pace, side by side.

items.name: TSS Earnslaw Steamship Cruise to Walter Peak
items.description: The 1912 'Lady of the Lake' is the only hand-fired coal steamship still carrying passengers in the Southern Hemisphere, a 90-minute glide across the water to Walter Peak High Country Farm, engine room open to wander and a pianist on deck. At the farm, a gourmet barbecue and a sheep-shearing show delight children while elders relax by the fire; ask for the vegetarian menu in advance.

items.name: Queenstown Gardens & Lakefront Peninsula
items.description: A leafy peninsula reaching into Lake Wakatipu, threaded with rose gardens, giant sequoias, a frisbee-golf course and easy flat paths right on the water, five minutes' stroll from the town centre. It is the gentle, unhurried heart of Queenstown: a picnic, a slow lakeside walk, and the mountains reflected on still mornings.

items.name: The Queenstown Lakefront & Steamer Wharf
items.description: The waterfront promenade is the town's living room, jetties, the historic Steamer Wharf, lakeside restaurants and the famous Fergburger queue just up the hill. Take an evening walk as the peaks turn pink, or hand the family a lakeside table for dinner with the water at your feet.

items.name: Shotover Jet
items.description: The only operator licensed inside the sheer Shotover Canyons, these red jet boats skim inches from rock walls at 85kph and spin the signature 360s down a river no other boat can run. A thrilling but accessible half-hour, the kind of adrenaline the teenagers demand and the parents secretly love.

items.name: Kawarau Bridge Bungy, the World's First
items.description: AJ Hackett opened commercial bungy jumping here in 1988; the 43m leap off the historic suspension bridge into the Kawarau River is where the whole sport began. Even if no one in the family jumps, the viewing decks and cantilevered platform make it a genuine pilgrimage, watch, cheer, and photograph the leap.

items.name: The Nevis Bungy & Swing
items.description: Reached by 4WD across private farmland, the Nevis is New Zealand's highest bungy, a 134m plunge from a pod slung over a canyon, plus the world's biggest swing, which arcs a vast 300m and can be ridden tandem. This is the serious adventurer's badge; for the rest, the drive and the canyon setting alone are extraordinary.

items.name: Shotover Canyon Swing & Canyon Fox
items.description: A 60m freefall from a 109m clifftop platform before a giant 200m swing sweeps you over the river, jumped forwards, backwards or in one of dozens of theatrical release styles. It sits in the sweet spot between bungy and pure fun, with the milder Canyon Fox zipline alongside for those who prefer to watch.

items.name: Skydive Over The Remarkables (NZONE)
items.description: Tandem jumps from 9,000, 12,000 or 15,000 feet fall over an almost unfair panorama, the lake, the alps and the fjords all at once. It is the once-in-a-lifetime photograph; and for family members staying on the ground, the drop zone viewing is part of the theatre.

items.name: White-Water Rafting the Shotover & Kawarau Rivers
items.description: The Shotover delivers grade 3–5 rapids down the legendary Skippers Canyon Road and through the dark Oxenbridge Tunnel; the Kawarau runs a gentler grade 2–3 for families and first-timers. A guided, full-day wilderness outing, choose the river to match your nerve.

items.name: Onsen Hot Pools & Day Spa
items.area: Arthurs Point, above the Shotover River
items.description: Private cedar-lined hot tubs perched over the Shotover gorge, where a garage-style wall slides open so you soak half-inside, half under the open alpine sky. Booked room by room, it is the discreet, restorative counterpoint to a day of adventure, a couples' soak, or the whole family unwinding with the mountains in view.

items.name: Gibbston Valley Wine Tour
items.description: Twenty-five minutes from town, Central Otago's 'Valley of the Vines' is world-famous for cool-climate Pinot Noir, its cellar doors strung along the Kawarau Gorge. A private-driver tour lets everyone taste freely, seated fireside at Amisfield, or deep inside the country's largest wine cave at Gibbston Valley, over a long, unhurried lunch.

items.name: Gibbston Valley Winery, Wine Cave & Cheesery
items.description: The region's oldest vineyard, first vintage 1987, is now a small estate in itself, a candlelit tasting in New Zealand's largest wine cave, an on-site cheesery, a bistro and a luxury lodge and spa. A single, elegant stop that satisfies serious wine lovers and casual visitors alike.

items.name: Amisfield Cellar Door & Restaurant
items.description: A rustic converted woolshed turned into one of the country's most acclaimed dining rooms, where the celebrated 'Trust the Kitchen' tasting menu is paired with the estate's own Pinot. Reserve well ahead; it is the definitive long lunch, and the kitchen handles vegetarian and dietary requests with real care.

items.name: Arrowtown, Historic Gold-Rush Village
items.description: A jewel of a settlement on the gold-bearing Arrow River, its 1860s Buckingham Street lined with more than sixty preserved miners' cottages, boutiques and cafés. A gentle, walkable day of history and browsing, with the excellent Lakes District Museum for the curious and gold-panning in the river for the children.

items.name: Arrowtown Chinese Settlement
items.description: At the edge of town along Bush Creek stand the restored stone huts and Ah Lum's store of the Chinese gold-miners who arrived from 1866, a quiet, moving record of a community that was pushed to the town's margins. A short, thoughtful walk that gives Arrowtown's prettiness real depth.

items.name: Arrowtown in Autumn
items.description: For a few weeks in April and May the town's avenues of oaks, poplars and sycamores blaze gold and amber, one of the most photographed sights in the South Island, crowned by the Arrowtown Autumn Festival. Time a visit here and the whole family walks through a painting.

items.name: Glenorchy & Paradise
items.area: Head of Lake Wakatipu, 45km from Queenstown
items.description: The road to Glenorchy is itself one of the world's great drives, hugging the lake to a tiny township at the gateway of Mt Aspiring National Park and the valley literally named Paradise. Base a serene day here among braided rivers and beech forest, the setting for Lord of the Rings' Misty Mountains and Isengard.

items.name: Dart River Wilderness Jet Safari
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Te Wāhipounamu / Mt Aspiring National Park
items.description: A jet boat threads the braided, glacier-fed Dart through the heart of a UNESCO wilderness, with 360-degree spins and a guided walk through ancient beech forest and film locations. Faster than the TSS Earnslaw but far gentler than the Shotover, a scenic thrill that spans the generations.

items.name: High-Country Horse Riding at Glenorchy
items.description: Guided treks cross glacial rivers and open flats beneath towering peaks, from gentle walking-pace rides for beginners to longer back-country trails. It is a soft, cinematic way into landscapes most visitors only see from a boat, well suited to a mixed-ability family group.

items.name: Lord of the Rings 4WD Film-Location Safari (Nomad Safaris)
items.description: A half-day 4WD tour to the real Middle-earth, the Kawarau Gorge that became the Pillars of the Kings, Deer Park Heights and The Remarkables that stood in for the Misty Mountains, with gold-panning along the way. Minimal walking and small Land Cruiser groups make it easy for every age.

items.name: Lake Hayes Loop Walk
items.description: A flat, beautiful 8km circuit around a mirror-still lake famous for its reflections of the surrounding hills, about two to three easy hours, or a gentle e-bike. One of the district's most relaxing outings, and a lovely stop paired with an Amisfield lunch nearby.

items.name: Moke Lake
items.description: A hidden, horseshoe-shaped lake ringed by hills down a short gravel road, gloriously quiet and framed for still-water reflections at dawn and dusk. A peaceful picnic, an easy loop walk or a paddle, the local's antidote to the town's bustle.

items.name: Milford Sound Day Trip
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Te Wāhipounamu / Fiordland National Park
items.description: Rudyard Kipling's 'eighth wonder of the world', sheer cliffs, Mitre Peak and thundering waterfalls plunging into a dark fjord, cruised on a nature boat with dolphins, seals and penguins alongside. The classic full-day trip pairs a scenic coach through the UNESCO wilderness with the cruise; a private guide or a fly-cruise-fly upgrade turns the long day gracious.

items.name: Doubtful Sound Wilderness Cruise
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Te Wāhipounamu / Fiordland National Park
items.description: Deeper, wilder and far quieter than Milford, reached by boat across Lake Manapouri and a mountain pass, or by Air Milford's exclusive scenic flight, and famed for its 'Sound of Silence'. The connoisseur's fjord, for travellers who want the untouched over the iconic.

items.name: Milford Sound Scenic Flight (Fly-Cruise-Fly)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Te Wāhipounamu / Fiordland National Park
items.description: A 45-minute flight over the Southern Alps and glaciers to land at Milford, cruise the fjord, and fly home, often called the world's finest scenic flight, and a fraction of the driving day. The private, elevated way to see Fiordland when time and comfort matter.

items.name: Heli-Picnic on a Glacier
items.description: A helicopter tracks over Skippers Canyon and the edge of Mt Aspiring National Park to touch down on an ancient glacier or a secluded alpine spot such as Earnslaw Burn, where a fresh-produce picnic is laid out amid waterfalls and blue ice. The most private, discreet luxury Queenstown offers, bespoke catering, including vegetarian, arranged on request.

items.name: Scenic Helicopter Flight & Alpine Landing
items.description: Shorter flights sweep over the lake, The Remarkables and Cecil and Walter Peaks with a snow or summit landing, a gentle taste of the high country for those not ready for a full heli-picnic. A superb way to give elders the alpine grandeur without a hike.

items.name: Routeburn Track Guided Walk (Ultimate Hikes)
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Te Wāhipounamu / Mt Aspiring & Fiordland National Parks
items.description: One of the world's ten classic hikes, a 32km alpine crossing of beech forest, high passes and hanging valleys, done as a guided full-day taste or a three-day lodge-based journey with all meals, packs carried and warm beds each night. The soft, curated way to walk a Great Walk.

items.name: Guided & Heli Fly-Fishing for Trout
items.description: Gin-clear high-country rivers hold sight-fishable brown trout that can top ten pounds; a private guide walks you to spring creeks, or a helicopter drops you into pristine backcountry water no road reaches. A meditative, world-class pursuit for the angler in the family, bespoke and unhurried.

items.name: Coronet Peak Ski Field
items.description: The closest field to town on a fully sealed road, with wide open runs, a strong learners' area and New Zealand's only floodlit night skiing followed by après. Between roughly June and October it is the family's easy day on the snow; out of season, the summit road still rewards with sweeping views.

items.name: The Remarkables Ski Field
items.description: The mountain range that gives Queenstown its silhouette hides sheltered basins and one of the country's best beginner zones served by covered conveyor lifts. In winter it is a superb, uncrowded family day out; the drive up alone, in any season, is spectacular.

items.name: Cardrona Alpine Resort
items.description: The region's largest ski area and best all-rounder, reliably snowy, with terrain for every level and a beloved après scene, reached over the dramatic Crown Range Road, New Zealand's highest sealed pass. Worth the drive for a change of mountain, and a fine stop en route to Wanaka.

items.name: Wanaka & the #ThatWanakaTree
items.description: A calmer, more local-feeling lake town over the Crown Range, with a famous lone willow standing in the water, gentle waterfront walks and the quirky Puzzling World for children. An easy, pretty day trip that trades Queenstown's buzz for something more serene.

items.name: Roys Peak Track
items.description: New Zealand's most photographed viewpoint, a switchbacked ridge that opens onto Lake Wanaka and the Southern Alps at your feet, about a 16km, five-to-six-hour return climb. A serious but non-technical hike for the fit; start at first light to have the famous ledge to yourselves.

items.name: Aoraki / Mt Cook Day Trip
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Te Wāhipounamu / Aoraki-Mt Cook National Park
items.description: New Zealand's highest mountain and the country's finest alpine amphitheatre, reached on a spectacular drive past the turquoise glacial lakes of Pukaki and Tekapo. Long as a day trip, best flown, or broken with an overnight, but the Hooker Valley walk beneath the peaks is one of the country's great gentle hikes.

items.name: The Crown Range Road & Cardrona Hotel
items.description: New Zealand's highest sealed road switchbacks over the Crown Range with a lookout that takes in the whole Wakatipu Basin, pausing at the 1863 Cardrona Hotel, one of the country's oldest and most photogenic pubs. A scenic drive that is a destination in itself, easy for all ages with a driver.

items.name: Skippers Canyon Scenic 4WD
items.description: One of New Zealand's most dramatic and precipitous roads, cut by hand during the gold rush along sheer schist walls above the Shotover, driven only by licensed guides. A vertiginous, story-rich half-day of history and jaw-dropping scenery, no walking required.

items.name: Queenstown Trail, E-Bike the Lakes & Vineyards
items.description: A superb network of largely flat, sealed cycle trails links the lakefront, Lake Hayes, Arrowtown and the Gibbston wineries, with swing bridges over turquoise rivers along the way. On an e-bike it suits mixed fitness perfectly, pedal between cellar doors, with a support vehicle if you prefer.

items.name: Stargazing at Bob's Peak
items.description: From roughly March to October, expert astronomers set up high-powered telescopes at the gondola summit to tour the Milky Way and the Southern Cross under some of the clearest skies in the hemisphere. A calm, wonder-filled evening, and the Central Otago region as a whole holds Dark Sky status.

items.name: A Central Otago Day, Cromwell, Bannockburn & the Fruit Bowl
items.description: Beyond Gibbston, the wider Central Otago wine country around Bannockburn and Cromwell yields some of the world's most celebrated Pinot Noir amid a stark, sun-baked landscape, with the region's orchards famous for summer stone fruit and cherries. A quieter, connoisseur's wine day away from the tour buses.

items.name: Ziptrek Ecotours
items.description: A guided series of ziplines and treetop platforms threads the native forest below the gondola, blending gentle thrill with a genuine conservation story and huge lake views. A crowd-pleaser that spans ages, real fun for children with an environmental lesson folded in.

items.name: KJet, Lake & Rivers Jet Boat
items.description: Departing right from the town pier, this hour-long ride runs Lake Wakatipu and the Kawarau and Shotover Rivers with spins and speed but a milder edge than the canyon-bound Shotover Jet. The convenient, family-friendly jet-boat option, no transfer, straight off the waterfront.

items.name: Paragliding & Tandem Hang Gliding from Bob's Peak
items.description: Launch off the mountain above town and soar tandem over the lake with a certified pilot, floating gently down to the lakefront, the calmest way to fly, with none of the freefall. A serene, photogenic thrill for those who want the view without the adrenaline of a skydive.

items.name: Fergburger & the Queenstown Food Scene
items.description: The town punches far above its size on food, from the legendary Fergburger queue to fine dining, a serious craft-beer and cocktail scene, and increasingly good Indian restaurants for a taste of home. An easy, buzzy evening out; several kitchens cater well for vegetarian and Jain preferences with notice.

items.name: Jack's Point & Alpine Golf
items.description: One of the world's most scenic courses runs along the lake beneath The Remarkables, its holes framed by schist tors and open water, playable by visitors and paired with a fine clubhouse. A gracious, low-key day for the golfer in the party, with the mountains for company.

items.name: Amisfield
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025, Three Hats & Restaurant of the Year
Food & Wine Global Tastemakers, No. 3 International Restaurant
items.description: Vaughan Mabee's hyper-local, wild-and-endemic tasting menu at the Amisfield winery, New Zealand's most celebrated kitchen.

items.name: Sherwood
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025, Two Hats
items.description: Chris Scott's produce-driven cooking at the eco-minded Sherwood, much of it from the restaurant's own gardens.

items.name: Aosta
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025, Two Hats
Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025, Regional Restaurant of the Year
items.description: Ben Bayly's ode to Northern Italy through a Central Otago lens, a stone cottage on Arrowtown's historic main street.

items.name: Kika
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025, Two Hats
items.description: James Stapley's small, ever-improving Wanaka room, sharing plates that get better every year.

items.name: Rātā
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025, One Hat
items.description: Josh Emett's refined bistro in a garden courtyard off the mall, polished, seasonal, and reliably excellent.

items.name: Jervois Steak House
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025, One Hat
items.description: Serious steak on the waterfront, arguably the best cut in the province, done without fuss.

items.name: Botswana Butchery
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025, One Hat
items.description: A stalwart of adventure-capital dining, meat, game and a vast wine list in a clubby lakefront room.

items.name: Toast and Oak
credentials: Cuisine Good Food Awards 2025, One Hat
items.description: A wine-led kitchen doing considered, seasonal small plates, Queenstown's most food-and-wine-minded newcomer to the hats.

items.name: Eichardt's Bar
credentials: The bar of Eichardt's Private Hotel, a MICHELIN One-Key hotel (2025)
items.description: An 1867 lakefront institution, plush sofas, a roaring fire and Bollinger by the glass, inside the town's grande-dame hotel.

items.name: Little Blackwood
credentials: Best Bar in New Zealand, Hospitality New Zealand Awards for Excellence 2022
items.description: A polished, intimate cocktail room perched over Lake Wakatipu on Steamer Wharf, the town's most decorated bar.

items.name: Bardeaux
credentials: A long-established Queenstown institution, one of the town's largest whisky collections
items.description: A candlelit cellar bar with a great open fire, Queenstown's serious room for whisky, wine and a quiet nightcap.

plan.heading: 4 days in Queenstown, done well
plan.lede: A day-by-day shape for the trip, the pace we would set. Your advisor books the flights and the rooms; the days are yours.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Arrive and check into a lake-view suite at Matakauri Lodge, set above Lake Wakatipu with the Remarkables in full view.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Walk the Frankton Track along the shoreline, then a quiet tasting at Amisfield in the Gibbston Valley.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dinner at Amisfield's tasting menu, or return to Matakauri for the kitchen's set courses by the fire.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Scenic flight over the Southern Alps to Milford Sound, landing among the fiord's waterfalls.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Private boat cruise on Milford, then fly back over Sutherland Falls and the Darran Mountains.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Dine at Rata, Josh Emett's restaurant in town, for South Island produce done simply.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Morning at Kinross and Chard Farm, tasting the valley's Pinot Noir with the winemakers.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Lunch at Mount Difficulty in Bannockburn, then the historic gold-mining road to Arrowtown.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Aperitif at The Bunker, then dinner there, a small, low-lit room known to locals.

slots.label: Morning
slots.text: Guided heli-hike onto a glacier or the Remarkables ridgeline, weather permitting.

slots.label: Afternoon
slots.text: Unhurried lunch at Sherwood's garden restaurant above town before the drive to the airport.

slots.label: Evening
slots.text: Depart, or a final lakeside drink at Eichardt's Bar in the old lakefront hotel.

items.name: Queenstown central
items.description: Walkable, lively and on the lake; convenient but busy, best for a short stay.

items.name: Arrowtown
items.description: A restored gold-rush village twenty minutes out; suits those wanting charm and quiet.

items.name: Jack's Point / Kelvin Heights
items.description: Lakeside and residential across the bay; for travellers who want views and calm over walking to dinner.

events.name: Queenstown Winter Festival
events.note: Ten days of fireworks, street parties and mountain events opening the ski season.

events.name: Snow Machine
events.note: A multi-day alpine music festival paired with skiing at the resorts.

events.name: Arrowtown Autumn Festival
events.note: The old gold town celebrates its turning trees with markets and a heritage parade.

onGround.heading: On the ground
onGround.note: Dress in layers for fast-changing alpine weather; the quietest luxury sits across the lake at the Kelvin Heights or Jack's Point side, away from the town-centre bustle.

rows.label: Arriving
rows.value: Fly into Queenstown Airport (ZQN), where a private chauffeur meets you airside for the ten-minute transfer to town, or arrange a scenic helicopter lift straight to a lakeside lodge.

rows.label: Getting around
rows.value: A private driver-guide is the way to move between vineyards and trailheads, with helicopter charters for the high country and Milford Sound.

rows.label: Connectivity
rows.value: Coverage is strong in town but patchy in the mountains; a New Zealand eSIM (One NZ or Spark) loads before landing.

rows.label: Money
rows.value: The New Zealand dollar (NZD); cards and contactless are near-universal, cash rarely needed, and tipping is not expected.

rows.label: Climate
rows.value: Two distinct seasons: Dec-Feb is warm, long-lit and green for the lake and alpine walks; Jul-Aug is peak ski, cold and reliable snow. Avoid the Apr-May and Oct-Nov shoulders, when weather turns unsettled and many operators pause.

rows.label: Flights from India
rows.value: No direct service from India; connect through Singapore (Singapore Airlines to Christchurch/Auckland, then a short domestic hop to ZQN) or via Sydney/Brisbane on Qantas or Air New Zealand. Total door-to-door runs about 20-22 hours. Fly the long leg in Singapore Airlines or Qantas business/first, and hold a comfortable overnight in Singapore rather than a tight same-day connection into a small alpine airport.

rows.label: Health & safety
rows.value: No vaccinations required beyond routine; New Zealand is very safe and tap water is excellent. The real caution is altitude and cold on the ski fields and the sharp weather swings on alpine roads and hikes; adventure activities carry inherent risk, so use reputable operators.

rows.label: Dining, veg & Jain
rows.value: Vegetarian dining is easy and Queenstown is well used to plant-based diets, though strict Jain (no onion/garlic/root) needs a quiet word ahead. Indian food is present but limited for a town this small; The Bunker and Rata handle refined vegetarian menus well, and a couple of Indian kitchens in town cover a genuine craving.
